student_answer: TDD in English is Test-Driven Development, which is a mechanism for independent testing in the project process. First, there is the red test, meaning that the tests are failing because the implementation is not in place. Second, there is the green test, which indicates that the necessary methods have been implemented to pass the tests. The length of the code does not matter, only its functionality. Finally, there is the refactor stage, where the implementation is corrected to improve the code and its implementation. In other words, the functionality is not modified, but the code is adjusted to make it more dynamic. It is a cycle that starts with red -> green -> refactor. It helps us verify whether the implemented methods have been used in the tests and what is failing.
expected_answer: The TDD cycle consists of three stages: first, a test is written that fails (Red) because the functionality has not yet been implemented. In the second phase (Green), the minimum code necessary for the test to pass is developed. Finally, in the Refactor stage, the code is improved while keeping all tests green. This cycle is crucial as it promotes proactive development, ensuring that the produced code meets the specifications initially defined by the tests.

student_answer: TDD helps us verify that the implementation of the methods in the practice and their usage are correct. Initially, we test that the tests work, meaning they fail because there is no implementation. We then proceed to implement the methods and check their functionality, which means they would pass the tests successfully. We correct the code without changing its functionality and achieve refactoring. This is TDD. However, the traditional testing approach would involve implementing the methods of the practice and then executing them to see if they work or not. If it fails, the test method would be changed and executed again. In this approach, it would be very good practice to use git to keep track of the point in the tests where the execution stands.
expected_answer: TDD and the traditional testing approach fundamentally differ in their sequence and purpose. In TDD, tests are written before the code, serving as specifications and guides for development. In contrast, in a traditional approach, the code is developed first and then tested, which can lead to reactive verification. Additionally, in TDD, tests are mandatory and help prevent errors from the outset, while in the traditional approach, tests may be optional and are used to validate work that has already been completed.

student_answer: The good practices of TDD are: * The code for each test must be independent of each other. * The implementation must be clear, with comments explaining what each method does. * The implementation of each test, for each method to verify the test, must be independent of the others. * First, the test would be run in red to check its functionality; secondly, its functionality would be implemented, which would turn the test green. Finally, we would refactor to improve the code and its implementation without changing its functionality, for better usage and development. The impact of good practices in TDD would have a positive effect on software quality, as you are testing whether those tests work and verifying that the methods used are executed. In case they do not execute, we can check with the tests where exactly it is failing.
expected_answer: Good practices in TDD include writing only the necessary tests to make them fail, avoiding code duplication, and regularly refactoring. These practices ensure that development remains focused and efficient, reducing code complexity and improving maintainability. By following these guidelines, the creation of more robust and high-quality software is promoted, as each unit of code is backed by tests that guarantee its correct functioning.

student_answer: The TDD (Test Driven Development) cycle is a software development methodology that involves creating tests throughout the development process, allowing for clearer and simpler resolution of problems and bugs. It begins with a red test (an initial test that has its corresponding errors), followed by a green test (a test that works but is not yet perfect), and finally refactoring tests (tests that address each error until the code is perfect or nearly perfect). TDD offers several advantages when designing each function, such as granularity (testing with the smallest possible code fragments to easily identify any errors) and isolation (testing functions individually to see if they work on their own rather than testing them alongside the rest of the code).
expected_answer: The TDD cycle consists of three stages: first, a test is written that fails (Red) because the functionality has not yet been implemented. In the second phase (Green), the minimum code necessary for the test to pass is developed. Finally, in the Refactor stage, the code is improved while keeping all tests green. This cycle is crucial as it promotes proactive development, ensuring that the produced code meets the specifications initially defined by the tests.

student_answer: TDD (Test Driven Development) is a software development methodology in which a set of minimum tests or requirements is defined before starting to program. The process is divided into three phases: red, green, and refactor. The first phase (red) involves defining these initial tests, which establish minimum processes or goals that the program must meet to function correctly. Its name comes from the result that the tests yield if they are run at that moment: red. This is because, at that point, no code has been implemented that can pass the test. The second phase (green) is the implementation of the code. In this phase, the necessary functions are written so that the tests pass the various checks. They do not have to be perfect; they just need to pass the test (hence the name, the color that indicates the test has been approved). Finally, there is the refactor phase, named after the homonymous process. In this phase, the goal is to optimize and improve the code without altering the green state of the test achieved in the previous step. It could be said that this is where the final quality is reached. In general, its importance arises in well-defined and business-oriented products, as it provides a robust structure with clear specifications. However, for more open-ended products, this methodology may not make sense.
expected_answer: The TDD cycle consists of three stages: first, a test is written that fails (Red) because the functionality has not yet been implemented. In the second phase (Green), the minimum code necessary for the test to pass is developed. Finally, in the Refactor stage, the code is improved while keeping all tests green. This cycle is crucial as it promotes proactive development, ensuring that the produced code meets the specifications initially defined by the tests.

The third phase is the refactor phase, where tests are added and the class or function is improved with the goal of increasing test coverage. For example: The functionality to sum negative numbers is added, or an exception is added if a string is received instead of an int.

This cycle is crucial as it promotes proactive development, ensuring that the produced code meets the specifications initially defined by the tests.

This cycle is iterated over for the development of new functionalities of the program.

The next phase is called Green, which consists of fixing the previous red test by including the constructor code that causes the red phase to fail. The third phase of the TDD cycle, known as Refactor, involves taking the previous code from the green test and refactoring it, thereby improving both the code and the tests.
expected_answer: The TDD cycle consists of three stages: first, a test is written that fails (Red) because the functionality has not yet been implemented. In the second phase (Green), the minimum code necessary for the test to pass is developed. Finally, in the Refactor stage, the code is improved while keeping all tests green. This cycle is crucial as it promotes proactive development, ensuring that the produced code meets the specifications initially defined by the tests.

student_answer: TDD simplifies the traditional testing process by reducing it to three phases: Red, Green, and Refactor. expected_answer: TDD and the traditional testing approach fundamentally differ in their sequence and purpose. In TDD, tests are written before the code, serving as specifications and guides for development. In contrast, in a traditional approach, the code is developed first and then tested, which can lead to reactive verification. Additionally, in TDD, tests are mandatory and help prevent errors from the outset, while in the traditional approach, tests may be optional and are used to validate work that has already been completed.

student_answer: Error handling in a Vaadin application that consumes the SWAPI API is done through the Circuit Breaker pattern, which is a resilience pattern that prevents the application from continuing to make calls to an external API, in this case, SWAPI, when this API is repeatedly failing. This way, the server is protected, overload is avoided, and a better response is provided when the external system is unavailable. The states of the circuit breaker are Closed, where the system is functioning correctly and allowing requests; if failures occur, they are counted. The Open state occurs after surpassing N failures, at which point it is considered that the API is down, and requests are immediately halted (fail fast). The application can respond with an error code or provide cached data (fallback data). After a cooldown period, the next phase is reached, the Half Open state, where it is checked if the API has recovered. If it is functioning, it returns to the Closed state; if it fails, it returns to the Open state, and the wait time is increased (Exponential backoff). There are also different types of errors: network errors (for example, ConnectException, UnknownHostException, and SocketTimeoutException), data errors (JsonSyntaxException and NullPointerException), or application errors.

The @Entity annotation allows us to define a Java object as an entity of a relational database, which is directly linked to the @Table(...) annotation that enables us to relate that entity to a table in our database. The @Entity annotation also allows us to use annotations when defining the attributes of the Java class, following the same logic as when we create an SQL table, such as @NotNull to ensure the field is not null, @Unique to ensure the value is not repeated, etc. Additionally, it allows us to use automatic mapping from JSON to Java using the specific naming convention of each implementation, thus automating deserialization. This is key when developing our API, as it is organized by layers, and the repository is responsible for handling all possible requests we can make to the database. The repository pattern should be implemented in an interface where the methods we define will be the actual SQL queries we will perform on our database using a naming convention established by the library, using keywords like findByTipo1, etc. Then, the names of those functions are automatically transformed by Spring Boot into SQL, saving us the effort of writing the queries ourselves.

student_answer: Spring Boot is a framework from the Spring company that employs a layered architecture to manage the backend of software projects. Spring Boot uses an MVC (Model View Controller) architecture. - Model: Represents the characteristics of a model class, in this case: Pokemon.java. It contains the attributes of a Pokémon such as id, etc. - View: Represents what the user sees through a visual interface. Here are the UI components such as Button, Grid, Layouts, etc. The view of our application could be MainView.java. - Controller: Represents the application's logic. This is where the business rules are found, and it is where HTTP requests are managed with the API. Containers are running instances of images. A container contains all the instructions necessary to create an application. Docker is the de facto standard application in the world of containerization. Docker allows you to define, create, and run containers. Tomcat is the embedded server of Spring Boot that facilitates the deployment of Docker containers.
expected_answer: Spring Boot includes an embedded Tomcat to simplify deployment: instead of configuring an external application server, the application is self-executable as a JAR that contains the server. This eliminates the need to install and configure Tomcat separately. For Docker, this is revolutionary because the Dockerfile can simply execute java -jar app.jar without relying on complex base server images. The result is a lighter Docker image, easier to maintain, and faster to deploy. The application exposes ports (EXPOSE 8081 in the backend, 8080 in the frontend) that are mapped in docker-compose.yml. This feature is essential for achieving self-contained and portable containers.

student_answer: If the frontend accessed the database directly, the following problems would arise: In terms of security, if it accessed the database directly, it would need to know the credentials, which poses a risk since it is the outermost layer, and a malicious user could access these credentials and misuse them. On the other hand, we would also be violating the principle of separation of responsibilities, as the frontend's function is solely to display data. Additionally, we would have tight coupling, which is inefficient if in the future we want to switch from MySQL to PostgreSQL, as we would have to change the entire application. However, if the frontend does not access the database directly, this issue does not occur, and we can change the database by only modifying the backend. Finally, business rules would need to be duplicated, which would generate inconsistencies.
expected_answer: If Vaadin were to access the database directly, the layered architecture would be completely broken. The frontend would need to know details of the persistence (tables, columns, SQL), which would create strong coupling and make it impossible to change the database without redoing the UI. Additionally, there would be no intermediate layer to apply validations or business logic, allowing incorrect or inconsistent data to be inserted from the UI. Security would also be compromised by directly exposing the database engine to end users, which is critical. Finally, it would not be possible to scale the frontend and backend separately because they share the same data layer. The backend's REST API acts as a secure, stable, and versionable boundary between the two layers, ensuring low dependency and greater maintainability.

Another problem would be the inconsistency between the language used by the frontend, which is JSON, and the language used by the database, which is query language. This issue is resolved in the connectivity between the backend and the database thanks to the Java Persistence API.
expected_answer: If Vaadin were to access the database directly, the layered architecture would be completely broken. The frontend would need to know details of the persistence (tables, columns, SQL), which would create strong coupling and make it impossible to change the database without redoing the UI. Additionally, there would be no intermediate layer to apply validations or business logic, allowing incorrect or inconsistent data to be inserted from the UI. Security would also be compromised by directly exposing the database engine to end users, which is critical. Finally, it would not be possible to scale the frontend and backend separately because they share the same data layer. The backend's REST API acts as a secure, stable, and versionable boundary between the two layers, ensuring low dependency and greater maintainability.

student_answer: To answer this, we need to understand what a REST API is. These are the de facto standard in the development community for communication between distributed applications. Additionally, they have their own REST architectural principles: * Stateless: Each request contains all the necessary information. * Cacheable: Responses to requests can be checked to improve performance. * Client-Server: Clear separation of responsibilities. * Uniform Interface: The interface is consistent with HTTP requests. * Layered System: The system is developed in layers, transparent to the user. Spring Boot is simply a framework for building enterprise applications in Java that can self-configure. The @RestController annotation is responsible for connecting a Controller to the REST API we are using, so that the interface is directly connected to it. It differs from a traditional @Controller in that it is simply added at the beginning of each Java file we develop, so the system knows it is a Controller.
expected_answer: @RestController is a combination of @Controller and @ResponseBody that indicates that the methods return serialized data (JSON/XML) instead of HTML views. In the context of the Pokémon system, @RestController in PokemonController allows methods like getAllPokemon() to directly return List<Pokemon> which Spring serializes to JSON, making it easier for the Vaadin frontend to consume this data via RestTemplate. Knowing this, we can begin to explain it from the user's action, performed from the frontend (Vaadin interface), which is sent to the backend by consuming the REST API to make HTTP requests. Then, the backend (Spring Boot, which is responsible for initializing the server) receives the request made by the user and serializes it (converting from a Java object to JSON) to perform a structured query to the database using JPA (Java Persistence API), potentially utilizing Hibernate as its implementation. It is important that the layers are well-defined for several reasons. First, if one layer fails, the entire project does not fail. If the annotation were not present, when creating a new Pokémon from the Vaadin interface, this new Pokémon would be created with an ID that already exists in the database (in the absence of ID validations in the backend). As I mentioned, this would lead to problems when performing other operations with the database, such as retrieving a Pokémon by ID when there are multiple with the same ID. This could cause errors and unexpected responses from the system.

A Vaadin application uses a layered architecture. Typically, three layers are used: * Presentation layer for data and UI. This layer is responsible for displaying data and listening to user events. It communicates with the next layer via HTTP. * Business logic layer, backend. This layer communicates with both the frontend and the next data persistence layer. From an architectural standpoint, the frontend layer should never communicate directly with the data persistence layer. This possibility is, in itself, a serious architectural flaw in a Vaadin application. From a technical perspective, direct access from Vaadin to the database presents higher coupling and a lack of separation of responsibilities, such as the Single Responsibility Principle of SOLID. This constitutes a violation of good programming principles and project development practices. Finally, this possibility poses serious security issues. The Spring backend handles all strong validations, data access, user authentication, database access authorization, among other security responsibilities within an application. The frontend does not contain these mechanisms and therefore should not access the database for security reasons. The layer closest to the client should never interact with the database to avoid potential injections or attacks and exposure of credentials.

The database returns results mapped to Pokemon objects via JPA. The controller serializes these objects to JSON and sends them to the frontend. The separation is critical: Vaadin does not access the database directly (security), Spring Boot does not contain UI logic (reusability), and JPA abstracts the database (flexibility). This allows for changing technologies without affecting other layers.

student_answer: JPA (Java Persistence API) allows for the automatic mapping of Java objects to database tables used in memory. The advantages it offers are in development and testing environments, as it does not work with real data or directly with the database, but you can replicate it.
expected_answer: The @Table and @Column annotations explicitly define how the Pokémon class is mapped to the database. @Table ensures that the table has a specific name (pokemon) regardless of the framework's conventions, and @Column allows controlling properties such as mandatory fields (nullable=false), the exact name of the column, or additional constraints. This prevents errors when the schema changes, avoids reliance on automatic names that may vary between versions, and guarantees that the database structure is exactly what the developer expects. Additionally, it makes the code more explicit, understandable, and resilient to future changes.

student_answer: The frontend communicates with the backend through an HTTPS service, which consumes data from a REST API that retrieves data from the application's backend using the getAllPokemon method declared in the repository. If the connection fails, there should be exceptions in the code that display notifications indicating that it was not possible to obtain all the Pokémon and that the grid should be shown empty.
expected_answer: The PokemonService uses RestTemplate to make HTTP GET requests to the backend endpoint (http://localhost:8081/api/pokemon). The getForObject() method deserializes the JSON response into an array of Pokemon[] objects, which is then converted to List<Pokemon>. If the connection fails, the catch block captures the exception and displays a notification to the user using Notification.show() informing them of the error, returning an empty list (Collections.emptyList()). This exception handling is critical for the user experience, preventing application crashes. The architecture allows the frontend to continue functioning even if the backend is temporarily unavailable.

student_answer: The repository layer is responsible for data access and performing operations with it, such as (GET, POST, DELETE...). It is preferable to writing SQL queries because it is much easier to validate with endpoints in a development and testing environment than with queries.
expected_answer: The Repository pattern provides an abstraction that encapsulates data access logic. Instead of writing direct SQL, methods are defined in interfaces that extend JpaRepository, such as findByTipo1(String tipo) or findByLegendaryTrue(). Spring Data JPA automatically generates implementations based on naming conventions. This offers advantages: portability between databases without changing code, type-safety in Java instead of SQL strings, easier testing through mocks, and protection against SQL injection. The Repository acts as an intermediary between business logic and persistence, allowing the underlying database to be changed without affecting the application code.

student_answer: The annotation of the ID field in the Pokémon entity is crucial as it declares it as a primary key. Additionally, if that annotation were not present, the user would have to manually insert the ID when creating a new Pokémon, whereas with that annotation, the ID is auto-incremental.
expected_answer: The @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY) annotation indicates to JPA/Hibernate to automatically generate a unique identifier for each Pokémon using the database's auto-increment capability. Without this annotation, JPA would expect the user to manually provide the id, which would cause errors because: 1) The Vaadin frontend has no way to generate valid IDs, 2) Duplicate conflicts could occur, 3) Persistence in the database would fail. With the annotation, each new Pokémon automatically receives a unique sequential id, allowing the entire flow (user → Vaadin → REST API → Spring Boot → JPA → Database) to function without manual intervention.

student_answer: If Vaadin accessed the data directly, it would jeopardize the integrity of the program, the security of the data, and its robustness. To prevent this, an HTTPS service is used that makes queries through a REST API to the application's backend, which returns a JSON that is sent to the Vaadin frontend, and finally, the interface is refreshed to display the data.
expected_answer: If Vaadin were to access the database directly, the layered architecture would be completely broken. The frontend would need to know details of the persistence (tables, columns, SQL), which would create strong coupling and make it impossible to change the database without redoing the UI. Additionally, there would be no intermediate layer to apply validations or business logic, allowing incorrect or inconsistent data to be inserted from the UI. Security would also be compromised by directly exposing the database engine to end users, which is critical. Finally, it would not be possible to scale the frontend and backend separately because they share the same data layer. The backend's REST API acts as a secure, stable, and versionable boundary between the two layers, ensuring low dependency and greater maintainability.

student_answer: The importance of validating inputs in TDD is necessary because it implements code with verified data. For example, if we are checking students at a university, a student cannot have negative years (-0 years). Similarly, when checking a student's ID, we need to verify if that ID exists, the student, etc. It is important to validate this data to create a good project and quality software to be tested with TDD, as it will ensure that the tests implemented in the code are reliable.
expected_answer: Validating inputs is crucial in TDD because it helps prevent errors and unexpected behaviors in the software. By writing tests to validate inputs before implementing business logic, appropriate conditions for the code's operation are ensured. This translates into more robust software, as runtime error cases are minimized. Validation in TDD not only improves code quality but also facilitates its maintenance and understanding.

student_answer: Environment variables must be declared in our Docker, as they will be used by our application. This is really important because these environment variables assign the necessary keys for integration with the database, that is, the username and password to access the database, among other relevant variables.
expected_answer: Environment variables in Docker Compose allow configuring services using external values defined in environment or .env files, avoiding hardcoding credentials and facilitating work with different environments through flexible, secure configuration that is separate from the code, which improves portability and maintainability.

student_answer: Docker Compose has lower complexity when it comes to deployment, but it falls short in terms of handling options compared to Kubernetes in complexity. Additionally, Docker is a private license that requires payment, whereas Kubernetes is free.
expected_answer: Docker Compose is a simple tool aimed at local development that uses basic YAML to deploy multi-container applications on a single host, while Kubernetes is a complex production platform that manages clusters, auto-scaling, high availability, and advanced orchestration through multiple resources and policies.

student_answer: Assertions in tests are used to execute the already implemented tests. They are added and executed to validate their functionality. That is, for example, a test is added, implemented, and by using assertions, it is executed, thus checking its behavior against the test.
expected_answer: Assertions are statements that verify whether a condition is true in tests. They are crucial because they allow developers to check the behavior of the code under test, ensuring that it produces the expected results. In TDD, assertions guide development by providing immediate feedback on whether the code meets the specified requirements. Using a variety of assertions, such as equality, nullity, and exceptions, enriches the testing process and helps to detect errors more effectively.

student_answer: Good practices are: - Have environment variables declared for everything that can be used. - Have, if possible, one container for each microservice of our application, as this prevents one failure from taking down the rest of the applications. - Use Docker volumes to improve the security of our host machine.
expected_answer: Best practices include using Compose without the version key, keeping YAML files clean and organized, creating lightweight images with multi-stage builds, managing configuration through environment variables and .env, avoiding credentials in the code, and using volumes, networks, and non-root users to achieve secure, reproducible, and maintainable environments.

student_answer: Docker volumes are virtual disk partitions that allow containers to store data without needing to request storage from the host disk.
expected_answer: Volumes in Docker are persistent storage areas managed by Docker that are mounted at internal paths of the container to retain data even when containers are deleted or recreated; they allow for the separation of data from the container, sharing information between services, and securely and portably managing critical databases and files.

student_answer: Maven would be installed, and commands could be used to check the functionality of the tests. We would use mvn test to run all implemented tests. We could use mvn test TestName to check the specific test we want to verify. This way, we can examine the behavior and see and correct the test failure. On the other hand, we can use the report provided by JaCoCo to verify the functionality of the tests.
expected_answer: Testing frameworks in Java, such as JUnit and Mockito, are essential for efficiently implementing TDD. They provide the necessary tools to write and execute tests, facilitating the creation of unit and integration tests. JUnit, for example, offers annotations that organize tests and allow for environment configuration, while Mockito enables the creation of mocks that simulate object behaviors. These frameworks contribute to the automation of the testing process, helping developers maintain an effective TDD cycle and ensure software quality.

student_answer: @RestController is used to manage HTTP requests from the backend controller. In this case, the controller is responsible for consuming the Pokemon API and deserializing the JSON text into Java objects, using the Jackson library. It then communicates with Pokemon.java to represent the Pokémon according to the model established in Pokemon.java. In Pokemon.java, @Entity maps the Pokémon into rows using an SQL table thanks to the Hibernate implementation of JPA. A traditional @Controller is found in the frontend and is used to consume the REST API from the backend. In this case, the backend communicates with the frontend to serialize Java objects into JSON format. Then, the frontend controller communicates with MainView or the frontend views to represent the Pokémon and their attributes in HTML tables.
expected_answer: @RestController is a combination of @Controller and @ResponseBody that indicates that the methods return serialized data (JSON/XML) instead of HTML views. While a traditional @Controller returns view names that are resolved to HTML templates, @RestController automatically serializes Java objects to JSON for HTTP responses. In the context of the Pokémon system, @RestController in PokemonController allows methods like getAllPokemon() to directly return List<Pokemon> which Spring serializes to JSON, making it easier for the Vaadin frontend to consume this data via RestTemplate. This distinction is fundamental for building modern REST APIs that separate data presentation.

student_answer: Code coverage is linked to the relevance of TDD because we can see the lines of code we have implemented and how they function. We can check where the tests are failing and correct them. However, the definition of the concept of code coverage is the metric that observes the percentage of success of the tests implemented in the project; the higher the percentage, the more tests have been conducted and verified. In other words, it measures the percentage of source code implemented along with the tests performed.
expected_answer: Code coverage is a metric that indicates what percentage of the source code is being executed during tests. In the context of TDD, high code coverage is relevant because it suggests that most of the software logic has been tested, which contributes to early error detection and confidence in the quality of the final product. Tools like JaCoCo help measure this coverage, allowing developers to identify untested areas.

student_answer: Health checks are a control mechanism that developers can access to receive information about the status of their application, meaning it checks if the database is available or if all microservices can communicate with each other, etc.
expected_answer: Health checks in Docker Compose perform periodic checks within the container to verify that the service is functioning correctly and not just that it is running; they allow for early failure detection, automate restarts, and make decisions based on the health status of the services, improving the resilience and availability of the system.

student_answer: First of all, it is important to use TDD to verify the functionality of the implemented tests. Secondly, the first test performed will fail because there are no tests implemented to check its functionality. It is essential that this test fails before implementation to ensure that these tests have been created and their functionality can be verified. The goal is to check the functionality of the individual implementation of each test in the project; therefore, it is necessary to know if those unimplemented tests work correctly and if their behavior has not been modified. These tests help the evolution of the system since we can verify its functionality at each point and improve or correct it depending on the test results. It is also important for communication among project members, as each test can be verified and any failures can be corrected wherever they occur.
expected_answer: The fact that a test initially fails is essential because it validates that the testing process is active and that the system does not have prior implicit behavior. This failure confirms that the test is correctly set up to detect the absence of the expected functionality. In TDD, this ensures that development is guided by clear specifications, avoiding assumptions. Furthermore, by requiring tests to be written first, it promotes a more modular and responsible design, as developers must think about use cases from the outset. This practice also improves communication between teams: tests act as living documentation of the expected behavior, facilitating collaboration, continuous integration, and early error detection. Thus, the Red-Green-Refactor cycle not only ensures coverage but also architectural coherence.

student_answer: Spring Boot along with MariaDB allows us to create an SQL database where we can store everything pertinent that our container needs, as it will send requests to obtain the data it requires. One way to achieve this is by compiling the application; if the database is not created, it will be created using the script we have prepared for that purpose. This ensures that it is always available during startup. In addition to this, to ensure everything is in order, dependency mechanisms and health checks are used to require that access to a database has been established before the application can start correctly.
expected_answer: The availability of MariaDB before starting Spring Boot is ensured through depends_on combined with health checks that validate that the database accepts connections; this prevents startup failures and makes the startup more robust, while Actuator provides additional health checks to monitor the service's status during and after startup.

student_answer: This is carried out in the following way: - Interaction: The user clicks on a UI element and creates an event. - Process: An HTTP request is sent to the SWAPI API, and it returns a JSON. - Update: The controller is responsible for communicating with the model to check the format of the data and then correctly modify the view or user interface.
expected_answer: The creation of a UI component in Vaadin, such as a form to search for characters from SWAPI, begins by defining the component in the MainView class. This component may include elements like TextField for user input and Button to trigger the search. When the button is clicked, a method is invoked that calls the SwapiService, which in turn uses the HttpClient to make the request to the SWAPI API. The service processes the response and, using GSON, converts the received JSON into Java objects that represent the characters. Finally, the data is displayed in a UI component, such as a Grid, which allows users to view the information in a structured manner. This process ensures a smooth integration between the user interface and the business logic.
